heading: Penal colony, prison and battleground
body: For most of its documented history, the Andaman and Nicobar archipelago figures in the historical record less as a place people lived than as a place people were sent. The British established a penal settlement at Port Blair, and between 1896 and 1906 built the Cellular Jail — a purpose-designed prison of solitary cells radiating from a central tower — to hold Indian political prisoners convicted for the freedom movement. Its inmates, transported there specifically to be cut off from the mainland, included some of the era's most prominent revolutionaries; the jail operated as an active penal settlement until the late 1930s and was formally closed in 1945.

The islands' history took an abrupt turn during the Second World War. Japanese forces occupied the Andaman and Nicobar Islands from March 1942 to October 1945, releasing the Cellular Jail's remaining prisoners but subjecting the population to a harsh occupation — forced labour on military construction, mass arrests of suspected spies, and, especially on Car Nicobar, brutal reprisals; roughly 2,000 residents are estimated to have died as a result of the occupation. On 30 December 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose, leading the Japanese-backed Provisional Government of Azad Hind and its Indian National Army, hoisted the Indian tricolour at Port Blair — the first time the flag of an independent Indian government flew on Indian soil — and briefly renamed the islands Shaheed and Swaraj, though real administrative control stayed with the Japanese military.

The islands returned to Indian administration after the war and became a Union Territory of independent India. The sites mapped here follow that double history: the Cellular Jail and its associated freedom-movement memory, and the wartime occupation that briefly made this remote archipelago the stage for a rival claim to Indian sovereignty.
